extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (discrete mathematics / introductory number theory) and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, algorithms and worked examples about equivalence relations, set partitions, congruence/modular arithmetic, divisibility (gcd/lcm), Euclidean and extended Euclidean algorithms, Bézout, and related lemmas. Material is aimed at teaching students how to define, prove, compute and apply these concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalence relation on a set is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show a relation is an equivalence relation, check the three properties individually with direct arguments or algebraic manipulation (examples: congruence modulo n, 'same age' relation). Use Theorem 9.2.6 as reference. Examples and explicit proofs are given for several relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes and representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalence classes partition the underlying set; for congruence modulo n the classes are [0], [1], ..., [n-1]. When representing classes modulo n one typically uses the smallest non-negative integer representative (the remainder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Euclidean division to identify the remainder r with 0 ≤ r < n so any integer n is in exactly one class [r]. Beware confusion with the programming % operator (see Warning 9.4.1): remainders and equivalence classes are related but not identical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a partition
rubrics_metrics.description: A partition 𝒫 of a set A is a collection of non-empty subsets of A so that every element x ∈ A belongs to some X ∈ 𝒫, and for X,Y ∈ 𝒫 either X∩Y = ∅ or X = Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, the union of the parts equals A and parts are pairwise disjoint. The elements of 𝒫 are called blocks, parts or pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes form a partition (and converse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation R on A, the set of equivalence classes {[x] | x ∈ A} forms a partition of A. Conversely, a partition of A defines an equivalence relation by x ℛ y iff x,y lie in the same part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs show (i) every element lies in its own class and (ii) distinct classes are disjoint (Corollary 9.3.7 used). For the converse, verify reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity by using membership in partition pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Congruence modulo n on Z is an equivalence relation whose classes are the residue classes modulo n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Euclidean division to represent integers and show each integer is congruent to exactly one of 0,...,n−1. Examples: classes modulo 4 listed explicitly. Use Theorem 9.2.6 as justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular arithmetic respects addition, subtraction, multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: If c ∈ [a] and d ∈ [b] (mod n) then c + d ∈ [a + b], c − d ∈ [a − b], and c·d ∈ [a·b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures operations on representatives induce well-defined operations on classes; proofs are straightforward algebraic manipulations (Theorem 9.4.2, Corollary 9.4.4). Examples illustrate computations like [7]·[9] = [3] (mod 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-definedness of operations on equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions [a]+[b] = [a+b], [a]−[b] = [a−b], [a]·[b] = [a·b] must not depend on choice of representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show if a'∈[a], b'∈[b] then [a'+b'] = [a+b], etc., using Theorem 5.3.3 / 9.4.2. Worked examples verify consistency across different representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning about modulo operator vs equivalence class
rubrics_metrics.description: The programming '%' operator gives the integer remainder; representing equivalence classes by remainders is common but thinking of 'modulo n' as an operation on integers can be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the smallest non-negative representative when convenient, but be deliberate when mixing moduli or relying on % semantics; the text warns of possible confusion and gives an example where a coauthor chose a different representative convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining equivalence classes from relations (geometric example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given relation (a,b) ℛ (c,d) ⇐⇒ a + d = c + b on R^2, the equivalence class of (a,b) is the line of slope 1 passing through (a,b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret relations algebraically to describe geometric or structural form of classes (example demonstrates how algebraic relation yields linear subsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modular arithmetic for error-checking (Luhn algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Luhn algorithm: given digits, double every second digit from the right, sum the digits (splitting doubled two-digit numbers), multiply sum by 9 and take modulo 10 to produce a check digit appended to the number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps are given with examples; the algorithm detects many common transcription errors (single-digit substitution, many transpositions) though not all. Practical application: credit-card and similar check digits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem (application note)
rubrics_metrics.description: One can compute arithmetic modulo several pairwise-coprime moduli (e.g., primes) and reconstruct an integer result using the Chinese Remainder Theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note and recommendation to see number theory course for full treatment; indicates usefulness for computing with large numbers via residues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear congruence solvability / multiplicative inverse existence criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The congruence [a]_n · [x]_n = [1]_n has no solution if a and n have a common divisor d > 1; conversely a solution exists iff gcd(a,n) = 1 (Bézout / extended Euclidean algorithm gives inverse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 9.4.8 proves impossibility when gcd>1. Remark 9.4.9 notes Bézout’s identity and the extended Euclidean algorithm compute the inverse when gcd=1; examples solving modulo 4 and 5 illustrate the criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear congruent generator (pseudo-random number generator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear congruential generator has recurrence x_{k+1} ≡ a x_k + c (mod n); appropriate choices of a, c, n can produce sequences that appear random but are deterministic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: poor parameter choices can lead to trivial cycles (example: a=7,c=5,n=11 yields constant sequence). Text recommends careful testing and further reading for randomness properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of gcd, lcm, and coprime
rubrics_metrics.description: gcd(a,b) is the largest positive integer dividing both a and b; lcm(a,b) is the smallest positive integer divisible by both; a and b are coprime if gcd(a,b)=1. gcd(a,0)=a (with conventions discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks cover special cases involving zero and conventions used. Use these definitions when simplifying fractions and solving divisibility problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic gcd identities used in Euclidean algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: For a,b ∈ N with a ≥ b: gcd(a,0)=a; gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a−b); if a = q b + r then gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equalities (Lemma 9.5.4) underpin the Euclidean algorithm; proofs use divisibility arguments and antisymmetry of ≤.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean algorithm for gcd (algorithmic steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithm: given integers a,b (|a| ≥ |b|), if b=0 gcd=a; else write a = q b + r with 0 ≤ r < |b| and repeat with (b,r) until remainder 0; final nonzero entry is gcd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Termination is guaranteed because remainders strictly decrease and are nonnegative integers. Worked examples (e.g., gcd(268,120)) illustrate the stepwise reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bézout's lemma (express gcd as integer combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: For integers a,b not both zero, there exist x,y ∈ Z such that gcd(a,b) = a x + b y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof obtained by running the Euclidean algorithm back or via induction on the sequence of remainders; the construction yields coefficients x,y explicitly (used in many subsequent results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended Euclidean algorithm (compute Bézout coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended Euclidean algorithm computes gcd(a,b) and integers x_n,y_n with gcd(a,b) = a x_n + b y_n by tracking quotient sequence q_i and recurrences x_{k+1} = x_{k−1} − q_{k+1} x_k, y_{k+1} = y_{k−1} − q_{k+1} y_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial values and recurrence are given; worked numeric example illustrates computing the Bézout coefficients explicitly (Algorithm 9.5.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid's lemma (prime factor divisibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is prime and p | ab, and p ∤ b, then p | a. More generally, if d | ab and gcd(d,b)=1 then d | a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs given: one using Bézout's lemma (write dx + by = 1 then multiply by a) and a more classical proof using the well-ordering principle and minimality arguments. Use this lemma in uniqueness of prime factorization and other divisibility arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between gcd and lcm
rubrics_metrics.description: For integers a,b the identity gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b) = |a·b| holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs L = |ab|/d with d = gcd(a,b), shows L is a common multiple and minimal via Bézout's lemma; demonstrates how gcd and lcm interact multiplicatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic (unique prime factorisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every integer n > 1 can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way (up to permutation of the primes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement given (Theorem 9.6.1) with historical remarks. The textbook indicates the theorem will be proved later; Euclid's lemma and previous divisibility results are prerequisites.
